title: Credit cards +9.88% YoY — fastest growth in 18 months
body: Credit cards outstanding grew 9.88% year-on-year in Jul 2026, up 0.31 points from 9.57% prior period. YoY growth re-accelerated for the sixth consecutive period: 8.0% in Mar 2026 → 8.1% in Apr 2026 → 8.5% in May 2026 → 9.6% in Jun 2026 → 9.9% in Jul 2026. The rate is now at the maximum level in the 19-period range.
implication: Credit card growth has fully reversed its deceleration trend and is now accelerating at the fastest pace in 18 months — the 9.88% rate is the strongest since Jan 2025 and confirms the purge-driven slowdown has ended. The six-period re-acceleration (8.0% → 8.1% → 8.5% → 9.6% → 9.9%) is the longest sustained acceleration in the dataset, and the 9.88% rate is only 0.5 points below the Jan 2025 peak, signaling the market is on track to return to near-double-digit growth within one period.

title: CC spend YoY — ecommerce 27.5% vs in-store POS 20.7%
body: On a year-on-year basis, credit card ecommerce transaction volume grew 27.5% and in-store POS volume grew 20.7% as of Jul 2026. Year-on-year removes the heavy seasonality in the monthly numbers — online is outpacing in-store on a clean comparison.
implication: Credit card spend is growing across both channels year-on-year (ecom faster). A spend mix tilting online is a mix of more card-not-present volume, where fraud and dispute rates run higher — so the channel mix carries risk information the headline spend growth does not.

Online (CNP) is the faster-growing channel on a year-on-year basis
Channel mix shift changes the fraud and dispute profile — risk models must track mix, not just total spend

implication: Foreign banks (Amex, Standard Chartered, etc.) traditionally served high-income customers — high credit limits, frequent international travel, premium cards. title: PSB banks hold 63.7% of debit cards — Payments gaining share in Jul 2026
body: Public sector banks account for 63.7% of total debit cards outstanding in Jul 2026 (-0.1pp vs prior month). Private banks hold 25.9%. Payments banks are the fastest-growing category (+0.1pp share gain).
implication: PSBs (government-owned banks like SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda) hold 63.7% of debit cards, largely because of Jan Dhan — the government scheme that opened basic bank accounts for millions of low-income households. If you're using debit transaction data for credit assessment, PSB debit data needs to be treated very differently from, say, HDFC or Kotak debit customers.

title: Gap: DC ATM cash at 80.0% of DC volume — digital transition is incomplete
body: Despite growth in digital payments, ATM cash withdrawals still account for 80.0% of total debit card transaction volume in Jul 2026 (-0.4pp vs prior month). DC ecommerce is only 5.4% of DC volume. India's debit card base remains overwhelmingly cash-dependent.
implication: 80.0% of debit card spending is ATM cash. Cash leaves no digital record — you can't tell where it was spent or on what. For lenders trying to assess a debit card holder's financial behaviour, the transaction history is mostly blank. Bureau scores (CIBIL, Experian) remain the primary tool for this segment — debit transaction data alone isn't enough yet.

title: UPI QR codes 16.7% YoY — stable growth, 14-month run
body: UPI QR codes grew 16.72% year-on-year in Jul 2026, down 0.15 points from 16.87% in Jun 2026. YoY growth eased 16.9% → 16.7%, a marginal 0.2-point decline — the rate has held in the 15–18% range for 15 consecutive months, with Jul's 16.7% near the median of 16.3%.
implication: The 16.7% YoY rate confirms UPI QR deployment remains in a stable, high-growth phase — the longest sustained expansion run in the acceptance infrastructure dataset. The rate has neither accelerated nor decelerated materially for over a year, suggesting the channel is absorbing new merchant adoption at a steady pace despite the large base. UPI QR is the only acceptance infrastructure segment with sustained double-digit growth.

The rate has stabilised near the median of 16.3% across the 19-period series, with no acceleration or deceleration trend visible since Apr 2025.
This sustained mid-teens growth indicates the network is adding 11–12 crore codes annually without saturation, even as the installed base has risen above 80 crore codes.

title: POS terminals mix rotating toward Public Sector Banks (+4.69 pp share in a year)

implication: This is a composition read: it says where the mix is shifting, not why and not what happens next. Watch whether Public Sector Banks holds its gains next month before reading the shift as a trend.

Rotation mass — the share that changed hands — is 4.70 pp.

title: Private Sector Banks took 70.3% of all new credit cards in the past year
body: Of the credit cards added over the past twelve months, Private Sector Banks took 70.3% — the largest share of the new money — growing 9.8% a year and accelerating (+0.09 pp). The rest went to Public Sector Banks 21.6%; Small Finance Banks 10.7%; Foreign Banks -2.6%. Foreign Banks took -2.6% while growing -6.5% a year and slowing (-0.58 pp) — a smaller slice of a faster-growing total, not a retreat.
implication: Shares of new lending move far faster than shares of the book, so this is the earlier read of the two. It says where the money went, not why — and a falling share alongside rising growth means the others grew faster, not that this one shrank.

chain: Every sector's credit cards is compared with the same month a year earlier, and each one's share of the total increase is taken.
Private Sector Banks accounts for 70.3% of the increase.
All sectors moved the same way this window, so the shares of the net increase are bounded and sum to a hundred.

title: Payment Banks shed ground to Public Sector Banks — the net barely moved
body: Debit cards shows almost no net change over the year, but a great deal happened underneath it: Public Sector Banks expanded while Payment Banks contracted by a similar amount. Public Sector Banks accounts for 33.1% of the total movement and Payment Banks for -27.7%. Almost none of that movement survives into the net figure — this period is a transfer between members, not a change in size.
implication: The headline number is the least informative part of this period. The reallocation between members is the finding.

chain: Each sector's change over the year is measured, then compared with the total movement ignoring direction.
Coherence — the net change divided by the total movement ignoring direction — is near zero here, meaning gains and losses very nearly cancel.
At this level a share of the NET change is not meaningful, so the reading is the transfer between members.

title: POS terminals shrank, but Public Sector Banks and Small Finance Banks moved against it
body: POS terminals fell over the past year, but not everywhere: Public Sector Banks and Small Finance Banks expanded while the rest contracted. Private Sector Banks accounts for 92.2% of all the movement in the period. Because parts moved in opposite directions, much of the movement cancels out and the net figure understates how much actually shifted.
implication: A shrinking total with members moving the other way is a different claim from broad decline. Read the members, not the headline.

title: Value transacted at POS grew while POS terminals deployed fell (-19.66 pp apart over a year)
body: POS terminals deployed and value transacted at POS normally move together — they are two readings of the same activity. Over the past year they have come apart. Value transacted at POS grew over the year; POS terminals deployed fell. Measured as POS terminals deployed minus value transacted at POS, the two year-on-year rates are -19.66 pp apart.
implication: A gap between POS terminals deployed and value transacted at POS is a question, not a conclusion: the two sides can part company because behaviour changed, because one side has a base effect, or because reporting shifted. Watch whether the gap closes next month — a pair that stays apart for several months is telling you the relationship itself has changed.

chain: POS terminals deployed and value transacted at POS are a declared pair: each side's growth is measured against the same month a year earlier.
Value transacted at POS grew over the year; POS terminals deployed fell.
The gap between the two rates — POS terminals deployed minus value transacted at POS — is -19.66 pp, wide enough to count as a divergence rather than ordinary drift.
